intro.title: Later: setTimeout and setInterval
intro.bodyMarkdown:
So far every line ran straight after the one before. Real programs often have to **wait**: for a timer, for a click, for data from a server. JavaScript doesn't stop and stare while it waits. It sets the job aside, carries on with the rest of the code, and comes back when the job is ready. Code that works like this is called **asynchronous**.

The simplest way to do something later is **`setTimeout(fn, ms)`**: run the function `fn` after `ms` milliseconds (1000 ms is one second).

```
console.log("Kettle on")
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("Tea is ready")
}, 1000)
console.log("Getting a cup")
```

Look at the order: `Getting a cup` shows **before** `Tea is ready`. `setTimeout` doesn't pause the program; it books the function for later and returns at once. Even `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs **after** the code that is already running has finished.

JavaScript does one thing at a time. It finishes the code it is running, then looks at its queue of jobs that are due (timers that have fired, clicks, data that arrived) and runs them one by one. This loop is called the **event loop**.

**`setInterval(fn, ms)`** runs `fn` again and again, every `ms` milliseconds, until you stop it. Both functions return an id; pass it to **`clearInterval(id)`** (or `clearTimeout(id)`) to cancel.

```
let count = 0
const id = setInterval(() => {
  count++
  console.log("tick", count)
  if (count === 3) clearInterval(id)
}, 200)
```

An interval that is never cleared runs forever, so always know when yours will stop. Here the run ends after the third tick, because nothing is left waiting.

intro.title: async and await
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Chains work, but there is an easier way to write them that reads like ordinary code, top to bottom: **`async`** and **`await`**.

Put **`async`** before a function, and inside it you can write **`await`** before a promise. `await` pauses **that function** until the promise settles, then gives you its value, as if it had been there all along:

```
function wait(ms) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms))
}

async function makeTea() {
  console.log("Kettle on")
  await wait(300)
  console.log("Water boiled")
  await wait(200)
  console.log("Tea is ready")
}

makeTea()
```

Compare it with the same steps as a `.then` chain: no nesting and no `return` to forget. Under the hood it is still promises.

Two things to know. First, an `async` function **always returns a promise**: whatever you `return` becomes that promise's value. So callers `await` it too, or use `.then`.

```
async function double(n) {
  return n * 2
}

console.log(double(4))
double(4).then((v) => console.log(v))
```

intro.bodyMarkdown:
Build the brains of a kitchen timer app. In the real app a "second" is 1000 ms; here a tick is just a few milliseconds, so the checks run quickly.

- `formatTime(seconds)` shows a time as `m:ss`, like `1:05`.
- `countdown(seconds, tick)` shows each time left, from `seconds` down to `0:00`, waiting `tick` ms between, then `Ding!`.
- `timers(list, tick)` runs several kitchen timers **at once**, and says which finished in what order.

```text
0:03
0:02
0:01
0:00
Ding!
```

You will need `wait(ms)`, which you wrote in this quest, and `await` in a loop.

challenges.title: Easy: Minutes and seconds
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `formatTime(seconds)` that gives `m:ss`: `formatTime(65)` is `"1:05"`, `formatTime(7)` is `"0:07"`.
challenges.hint: `Math.floor(seconds / 60)` minutes and `seconds % 60` seconds, padded with `padStart(2, "0")`.

challenges.title: Easy: Wait
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `wait(ms)`, a promise that is fulfilled after `ms` milliseconds, and use it to show `Start`, then `Stop` 50 ms later.
challenges.hint: `return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms))`; then `console.log("Start")`, `await wait(50)`, `console.log("Stop")`.

tests.label: wait waits
tests.assertion: (async () => { const t = Date.now(); await wait(40); return Date.now() - t >= 30 })()

challenges.title: Medium: Count down
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `async function countdown(seconds, tick)` that shows each time left with `formatTime`, from `seconds` down to `0:00`, waiting `tick` ms between, then shows `Ding!`.
challenges.hint: `for (let s = seconds; s >= 0; s--) { console.log(formatTime(s)); if (s > 0) await wait(tick) }`, then `Ding!`.

tests.label: countdown(3, 5)
tests.assertion: (async () => { const got = []; const log = console.log; console.log = (...v) => got.push(v.join(" ")); try { await countdown(3, 5) } finally { console.log = log } return JSON.stringify(got) === "[\"0:03\",\"0:02\",\"0:01\",\"0:00\",\"Ding!\"]" })()

tests.label: countdown(0, 5)
tests.assertion: (async () => { const got = []; const log = console.log; console.log = (...v) => got.push(v.join(" ")); try { await countdown(0, 5) } finally { console.log = log } return JSON.stringify(got) === "[\"0:00\",\"Ding!\"]" })()

tests.label: It waits
tests.assertion: (async () => { const log = console.log; console.log = () => {}; const t = Date.now(); try { await countdown(3, 20) } finally { console.log = log } return Date.now() - t >= 50 })()

challenges.title: Medium: Pause and stop
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `async function countdownUntil(seconds, tick, shouldStop)` that counts down like `countdown` (returning instead of showing), but before each tick checks `shouldStop()`: if it is true, return `"Stopped at M:SS"`. If it reaches zero, return `"Ding!"`.
challenges.hint: In the loop over `s`: `if (shouldStop()) return `Stopped at ${formatTime(s)}``, then `await wait(tick)`.

challenges.title: Hard: Several timers
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `async function timers(list, tick)`: `list` is like `[["eggs", 4], ["toast", 2]]`. Run every timer **at once** (each waits `seconds * tick` ms), and return the names in the order they finish.
challenges.hint: Keep `const done = []`. `await Promise.all(list.map(async ([name, s]) => { await wait(s * tick); done.push(name) }))`, then return `done`.

tests.label: At once
tests.assertion: (async () => { const t = Date.now(); await timers([["a", 5], ["b", 5], ["c", 5]], 10); return Date.now() - t < 120 })()

challenges.title: Hard: Announce each
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `async function announce(list, tick)` that runs the timers at once like `timers`, showing `NAME is ready!` the moment each finishes, and then `All done` once they all have.
challenges.hint: The same as `timers`, with a `console.log` instead of the `push`, and `All done` after `await Promise.all(…)`.

tests.label: Pasta and sauce
tests.assertion: (async () => { const got = []; const log = console.log; console.log = (...v) => got.push(v.join(" ")); try { await announce([["pasta", 5], ["sauce", 3]], 10) } finally { console.log = log } return JSON.stringify(got) === "[\"sauce is ready!\",\"pasta is ready!\",\"All done\"]" })()

tests.label: Nothing
tests.assertion: (async () => { const got = []; const log = console.log; console.log = (...v) => got.push(v.join(" ")); try { await announce([], 10) } finally { console.log = log } return JSON.stringify(got) === "[\"All done\"]" })()

choices.label: It is the only way to show text
Each step waits for the one before, so the loop reads in order

questions.explanation: await makes a loop that pauses.

choices.label: Await each in a for…of loop

intro.title: Medium side quest: A pizza order tracker
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A pizza shop wants its app to show each order moving through the kitchen. The kitchen's steps are async functions that are already written: `makeDough(pizza)`, `addToppings(base)` and `bake(raw)`. Each takes a little while, and `makeDough` fails for a pizza that isn't on the `MENU`.

You will write the code that drives them:

- `makePizza(pizza)`: the three steps in order, each using the result of the one before;
- `track(pizza)`: the same, with an update line after each step;
- `order(pizzas)`: make every pizza of an order at once, and the bill;
- `orderReport(pizzas)`: an order where some pizzas may fail, saying which.

```text
margherita: dough ready
margherita: toppings on
margherita: baked
```

challenges.title: Easy: One pizza
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `async function makePizza(pizza)` that runs `makeDough`, then `addToppings` on its result, then `bake` on that, and returns what `bake` gives.
challenges.hint: `const dough = await makeDough(pizza)`, and so on.

tests.label: Not on the menu
tests.assertion: (async () => { try { await (makePizza("pineapple")) } catch (_cq_e) { return (String(_cq_e?.name) + ": " + String(_cq_e?.message)).includes("No such pizza: pineapple") } return false })()

challenges.title: Easy: The price
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `function price(pizzas)` that returns the total price of a list of pizzas from `MENU`.
challenges.hint: `pizzas.reduce((sum, p) => sum + MENU[p], 0)`.

challenges.title: Medium: Track it
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `async function track(pizza)` that makes the pizza like `makePizza`, but returns the list of update lines: `PIZZA: dough ready`, `PIZZA: toppings on`, `PIZZA: baked`. If a step fails, the list ends with `PIZZA: problem - MESSAGE`.
challenges.hint: Push a line after each awaited step, all inside `try`; in `catch`, push the problem line. Return the list either way.

tests.label: A margherita
tests.assertion: (async () => JSON.stringify(await (track("margherita"))) === JSON.stringify(["margherita: dough ready", "margherita: toppings on", "margherita: baked"]))()

tests.label: Not on the menu
tests.assertion: (async () => JSON.stringify(await (track("kebab"))) === JSON.stringify(["kebab: problem - No such pizza: kebab"]))()

tests.label: Works with other data too

challenges.title: Medium: A whole order
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `async function order(pizzas)` that makes all the pizzas **at once** and returns `{ ready, bill }`: `ready` the list of baked pizzas in order, `bill` the total price.
challenges.hint: `const ready = await Promise.all(pizzas.map(makePizza))`; the bill as in `price`.

tests.label: Two pizzas
tests.assertion: (async () => JSON.stringify(await (order(["veggie", "pepperoni"]))) === JSON.stringify({ ready: ["veggie baked", "pepperoni baked"], bill: 21 }))()

tests.label: At once
tests.assertion: (async () => { const t = Date.now(); await order(["veggie", "veggie", "veggie", "veggie"]); return Date.now() - t < 180 })()

tests.label: Works with other data too

challenges.title: Hard: Some fail
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `async function orderReport(pizzas)` that makes them all at once but doesn't let one bad pizza spoil the order. Return `{ ready, failed, bill }`: the baked pizzas, the names that failed, and the price of only the ones that worked.
challenges.hint: `Promise.allSettled(pizzas.map(makePizza))`; go through the results with their index to sort them into ready and failed.

tests.label: One bad
tests.assertion: (async () => JSON.stringify(await (orderReport(["margherita", "sushi", "veggie"]))) === JSON.stringify({ ready: ["margherita baked", "veggie baked"], failed: ["sushi"], bill: 19 }))()

tests.label: All good
tests.assertion: (async () => JSON.stringify(await (orderReport(["pepperoni"]))) === JSON.stringify({ ready: ["pepperoni baked"], failed: [], bill: 11 }))()

tests.label: Works with other data too

challenges.title: Expert: One oven
challenges.promptMarkdown: The shop has only **one oven**: two pizzas can't bake at the same time. Write `async function busyNight(pizzas)` that prepares all doughs and toppings at once, then bakes the pizzas **one after another**, in order, and returns the baked pizzas.
challenges.hint: First `const raws = await Promise.all(pizzas.map(async (p) => addToppings(await makeDough(p))))`. Then a `for…of` loop that awaits `bake` for each.

tests.label: One at a time in the oven
tests.assertion: (async () => { const real = bake; let inOven = 0; let most = 0; bake = async (raw) => { inOven++; most = Math.max(most, inOven); try { return await real(raw) } finally { inOven-- } }; try { await busyNight(["veggie", "veggie", "veggie"]) } finally { bake = real } return most === 1 })()

tests.label: Works with other data too

questions.prompt: Why must `makeDough`, `addToppings` and `bake` run one after another for a pizza?

choices.label: JavaScript runs only one async function at a time
Each needs the result of the one before
They are too slow to run together

choices.label: There are many ovens in JavaScript
They don't depend on each other

choices.label: Rejects, so the whole order fails

questions.prompt: Which method lets the good pizzas through when one fails?
With one oven, how should the baking run?
questions.explanation: A shared resource means one at a time.

challenges.title: Easy: Get the JSON
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `async function getJson(url)`: fetch it with `fakeFetch`; if the response isn't `ok`, throw `Error("URL failed with STATUS")`; else return the parsed JSON.
challenges.hint: Check `response.ok`, then `return response.json()`.

tests.label: Paris
tests.assertion: (async () => { try { await (getJson("/weather/paris")) } catch (_cq_e) { return (String(_cq_e?.name) + ": " + String(_cq_e?.message)).includes("/weather/paris failed with 404") } return false })()

challenges.title: Easy: One line
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `function line(report)` that turns `{ city: "Oslo", temp: 8, sky: "rain" }` into `Oslo      8°C  rain`: the city padded to 8 characters, the temperature padded on the left to 3, then `°C`, two spaces and the sky.
challenges.hint: `report.city.padEnd(8) + String(report.temp).padStart(3) + "°C  " + report.sky`.

challenges.title: Medium: The board
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `async function board(cities)` that fetches every city's weather **at once** and returns a list of lines (using `line`). A city that fails gives `City: not available` instead, with a capital first letter.
challenges.hint: Map each city to an async function with its own `try`…`catch` that returns a line either way, then `Promise.all`.

tests.label: Three cities
tests.assertion: (async () => JSON.stringify(await (board(["lisbon", "oslo", "paris"]))) === JSON.stringify(["Lisbon   24°C  sunny", "Oslo      8°C  rain", "Paris: not available"]))()

tests.label: At once
tests.assertion: (async () => { const real = fakeFetch; let open = 0; let most = 0; fakeFetch = async (u) => { open++; most = Math.max(most, open); try { return await real(u) } finally { open-- } }; try { await board(["oslo", "seoul", "cairo"]) } finally { fakeFetch = real } return most > 1 })()

challenges.title: Medium: Summary
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `async function summary(cities)` that fetches the cities at once (skipping any that fail) and returns `{ warmest, coldest, average }`: the city names as the server writes them, and the average temperature rounded to 1 decimal place. With no cities known, return `null`.
challenges.hint: Use `Promise.allSettled`, keep the fulfilled values, then sort a copy by `temp` (or use `reduce`).

challenges.title: Hard: One more try
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `async function refresh(cities, getWeather)`: like `board`, but uses `getWeather(city)` (an async function giving a report) instead of fetching, and if it fails for a city, tries **once more** before showing `City: not available`. Return the lines in order.
challenges.hint: For each city: `try { return line(await getWeather(city)) } catch { try { return line(await getWeather(city)) } catch { return … } }`.

tests.label: A blip is retried
tests.assertion: (async () => { const tries = {}; const getWeather = async (c) => { tries[c] = (tries[c] ?? 0) + 1; if (c === "oslo" && tries[c] === 1) throw new Error("blip"); return { city: c[0].toUpperCase() + c.slice(1), temp: 5, sky: "fog" } }; const lines = await refresh(["oslo", "rome"], getWeather); return JSON.stringify(lines) === JSON.stringify(["Oslo      5°C  fog", "Rome      5°C  fog"]) && tries.oslo === 2 && tries.rome === 1 })()

tests.label: Gives up after two tries
tests.assertion: (async () => { let calls = 0; const lines = await refresh(["oslo"], async () => { calls++; throw new Error("down") }); return lines[0] === "Oslo: not available" && calls === 2 })()

challenges.title: Expert: Keep it fresh
challenges.promptMarkdown: Asking the server again for every redraw is wasteful, but weather does change. Write `makeCache(maxAge)`: it returns an async function `get(city)` that fetches `/weather/CITY` with `getJson`, but reuses a saved report for that city if it is younger than `maxAge` ms. Each `get` call returns the report.
challenges.hint: Inside `makeCache`, keep `const saved = new Map()` of city → `{ report, at }`. In `get`: if there is one and `Date.now() - at < maxAge`, return its report; else fetch, save with `at: Date.now()`, return.

tests.label: Reuses a fresh one
tests.assertion: (async () => { const real = fakeFetch; let calls = 0; try { fakeFetch = (u) => { calls++; return real(u) }; const get = makeCache(1000); await get("oslo"); await get("oslo"); await get("seoul") } finally { fakeFetch = real } return calls === 2 })()

tests.label: Fetches again when old
tests.assertion: (async () => { const real = fakeFetch; let calls = 0; try { fakeFetch = (u) => { calls++; return real(u) }; const get = makeCache(30); await get("oslo"); await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50)); await get("oslo") } finally { fakeFetch = real } return calls === 2 })()
